title: Fathers and Daughters 1: When a Father Is Present but His Daughter Still Feels Fatherless
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley launches a new series on how fathers shape their children, opening with the counterintuitive claim that shared activity between fathers and kids is not the same thing as closeness or secure attachment — a misconception he says is common among fathers and churches alike. He draws on Susan Schwartz's book The Absent Father Effect on Daughters, which blends psychoanalysis and social science, to argue fathers are 'decisive in the destiny of their children.' The piece's central, unsettling claim is that a father can be physically present in the home yet still leave his daughter feeling fatherless if he cannot 'see, regard, or be with her' emotionally — leaving a wound Schwartz describes as a rupture in the 'threads of her personality.' Bradley frames this as material that reshaped his own understanding of fatherhood.
points: Opens with a direct challenge to a common fatherhood myth: that doing activities together automatically produces closeness or attachment.
Introduces Susan Schwartz's psychoanalytic framework distinguishing physical presence from emotional attunement — a father can be 'present but absent.'
Uses a striking, quotable image ('a hole in her heart,' 'threads of her personality rupture') to describe what happens to daughters of emotionally unavailable fathers.
Frames this explicitly as a gap in pastoral training, positioning the series as corrective reading for fathers and church leaders alike.
quotes: shared activity between fathers and their children is not the same as closeness and attachment. This is one of the biggest misconceptions I encounter in discussions about fatherhood.
When children are securely attached to their fathers, they look to them for safety, comfort, protection, and emotional regulation.
Schwartz begins by observing that fathers are decisive in the destiny of their children.
When her father cannot see, regard or be with her, she has a hole in her heart; the threads of her personality rupture.
This book completely changed my views of fathers and daughters and what follows are things that I wished I had known before.
What Schwartz presents is not intuitive. If it were, many therapists would be unemployed.
